# Mohs Micrographic Surgery: Design and Execution of Secondary Intention

**Authors:** Tatiana V. Camayo, Maryam Feili

**Source:** StatPearls - StatPearls Publishing

## Abstract

Mohs micrographic surgery (MMS) is a widely used surgical technique primarily indicated for treating nonmelanoma skin cancers and select cases of melanoma, particularly in anatomically or cosmetically sensitive areas where maximal tissue preservation is desired. The reconstruction process after MMS usually requires skilled surgeons who can perform intricate flaps and grafting procedures. Second intention healing (SIH) is a surgical repair alternative that does not require movement of adjacent tissue for primary closure. SIH is still somewhat used across surgical specialties, mostly in cases where the clinical condition (infection, wound size, skin quality for primary closure) limits the reconstructive options. Mohs surgeons favored SIH as a repair method before the fresh tissue approach was developed. Most available data suggest that SIH is a cost-effective alternative with good cosmetic and functional outcomes. SIH was initially applied to convex surfaces such as the forehead but has since gained acceptance for use in several concave regions, including the lips and ears. Nonetheless, SIH after MMS is currently widely underused. To date, only approximately 25% (18% to 33%) of MMS defects are permitted to heal by second intention.[6] This underuse warrants greater attention and supports considering SIH as a primary option in select clinical scenarios where it may improve both cosmetic and functional outcomes, as discussed later in this activity, or in settings where more complex surgical procedures are unavailable or pose added risk.
